entry: Roman emperor (r. 527–565). His reign was marked by an ambitious but only partly realized *renovatio imperii* ("restoration of the Empire"). His general Belisarius conquered the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa, and Belisarius, Narses and other generals then took the Ostrogothic Kingdom, restoring Dalmatia, Sicily, Italy and [[Rome]] to the empire. These campaigns re-established Roman control over the western Mediterranean. A second war with the [[Sasanian Empire]] in the east was partly driven by his ambitions in the west. A [[Bubonic plague|bubonic plague]] outbreak in 541–542 ravaged [[Constantinople]] and beyond. His codification of Roman law, the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, remains the basis of [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]] in many modern states. He oversaw the reconstruction of the [[Hagia Sophia]] as a domed basilica from 532 to 537. His reign was troubled by religious conflicts between Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian Christians.

German chemist and agricultural scientist. He made major contributions to the theory, practice and teaching of chemistry, as well as to agricultural and biological chemistry, and is considered one of the principal founders of [[Organic chemistry]]. As a professor at the University of Giessen he devised the modern laboratory-oriented method of teaching chemistry. He emphasized [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]] and minerals as essential plant nutrients and popularized the law of the minimum, which holds that plant growth is limited by the scarcest nutrient resource rather than by the total amount of resources available. He has been described as the "father of the [[Fertilizer|fertilizer]] industry." He also developed a manufacturing process for beef extracts, and a company, the Liebig Extract of Meat Company, was founded to exploit it; it later introduced the Oxo brand beef bouillon cube. He popularized an earlier invention for condensing vapors, which became known as the Liebig condenser.

Italian professional football club based in Turin. Founded in 1897 by Turinese students, Juventus plays in [[Serie A]], the top tier of Italian football. It holds a record 36 Italian league titles and has won two European Cup/[[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]] titles. It won nine consecutive Serie A titles from 2012 to 2020. Owned by the Agnelli family since 1923, it is the most widely supported club in Italy.

Sub-Neptune exoplanet orbiting the [[Red dwarf|red dwarf]] K2-18, 124 light-years from Earth. It is about 2.6 times Earth's radius and has a 33-day orbit within the star's habitable zone. The [[James Webb Space Telescope]] detected [[Water vapor|water vapor]], [[Carbon dioxide]] and [[Methane]] in its atmosphere, data interpreted as indicating a water ocean beneath a hydrogen-rich atmosphere or a gas-rich mini-Neptune. K2-18b is the prototype for hycean planets, which have abundant water under a hydrogen envelope. A controversial 2025 report of dimethyl sulfide (DMS), a possible biosignature, has not been widely accepted, as abiotic processes could explain it and the detection is doubted.

Mountain in the Karakoram range, the second highest on Earth. At 8,611 meters (28,251 ft), it stands just below [[Mount Everest]] at 8,849 meters. It lies partly in Gilgit-Baltistan, in [[Pakistan]]-administered Kashmir, and partly in the [[China|China]]-administered Trans-Karakoram Tract of Xinjiang. Of the five highest mountains, it has long been the deadliest: before 2021, about one person died on it for every four who reached the summit. As of August 2023, an estimated 800 people had summited, with 96 deaths during attempted climbs. The first ascent, in 1954, was made by Lino Lacedelli and Achille Compagnoni on an Italian expedition led by Ardito Desio. In January 2021 it became the final eight-thousander to be climbed in winter. The name comes from the Great Trigonometrical Survey of British India, which labeled it K2, the second peak surveyed in the Karakoram.

American fast-food chain specializing in Southern fried chicken, a subsidiary of Yum! Brands. [[Colonel Sanders|Colonel Harland Sanders]] began selling fried chicken from a roadside restaurant in Corbin, Kentucky, during the Great Depression. He sold the company in 1964, and it became one of the first American fast-food chains to expand abroad. In 1987 it became the first Western restaurant chain to open in China, now its largest market. Its original product is pressure-fried chicken seasoned with 11 herbs and spices. Ownership passed through Heublein and R. J. Reynolds before [[PepsiCo]] acquired it.

Main security agency of the [[Soviet Union]], 1954–1991. Formed in March 1954 from the security directorates of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, after the fall of [[Lavrentiy Beria]], it succeeded the Cheka, OGPU and NKVD. Its duties included foreign intelligence, counterintelligence, border security, guarding the Soviet leadership and combating dissent. Its leaders included [[Yuri Andropov]], and chairman Vladimir Kryuchkov led the failed August 1991 coup in an attempt to depose President [[Mikhail Gorbachev]]. The KGB was dissolved on December 3, 1991, and succeeded in Russia by the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) and the Federal Security Service (FSB).

National airline of the [[Netherlands]], founded in 1919 and the oldest airline still operating under its original name. Its headquarters are in Amstelveen, and its hub is at [[Amsterdam Airport Schiphol]]. KLM was an early pioneer of scheduled intercontinental flights, including interwar routes to the [[Dutch East Indies]]. Since merging with Air France in 2004 it has formed part of the Air France–KLM group, though both carriers keep separate brands. KLM is a member of the SkyTeam alliance.

Multinational professional services network headquartered in [[London]], one of the Big Four accounting firms alongside [[Deloitte]], EY and [[PwC]]. As of December 2024 it operated as a network of 46 firms in 145 countries, employing 275,288 people. The name stands for Klynveld Peat Marwick Goerdeler, an initialism chosen when KMG merged with Peat Marwick in 1987. Its three main divisions are financial audit, [[Tax|tax]] and consulting.

Large, nocturnal, flightless [[Parrot|parrot]] endemic to [[New Zealand]]. It is the world's heaviest parrot and the only parrot with a polygynous lek breeding system. Introduced predators such as cats, rats, ferrets and stoats nearly wiped it out. Earlier conservation efforts were unsuccessful until the Kākāpō Recovery Programme began in 1995. The species is critically endangered, and in 2023 birds were reintroduced to the mainland at Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari.

Japanese Buddhist monk, calligrapher and poet who founded the esoteric Shingon school of [[Buddhism]]. He traveled to China, where he studied Tangmi, or Chinese [[Vajrayana]] Buddhism, under the monk Huiguo. Returning to Japan, he founded Shingon, the Japanese branch of Vajrayana, and with the backing of several emperors he preached its teachings and founded temples. He chose Mount Kōya as a holy site and spent his later years there. Born in Sanuki Province on [[Shikoku]], he is posthumously known as Kōbō Daishi. Legends credit him with inventing the kana syllabary, with which Japanese is still written in combination with [[Kanji|kanji]], and with the Iroha poem.

Historic German city, now [[Kaliningrad]], Russia. Founded in 1255 by the [[Teutonic Order]], it was named for King Ottokar II of Bohemia. A Baltic port and capital of the Duchy of Prussia, its university, the Albertina, founded in 1544, made it an intellectual center, home to philosopher [[Immanuel Kant]] and mathematician [[David Hilbert]]. The seven bridges problem posed by [[Leonhard Euler]] laid foundational work for [[Graph theory|graph theory]]. Heavily damaged in World War II, the city was annexed by the [[Soviet Union]] in April 1945, and its German population was expelled. It was renamed Kaliningrad in 1946 after Soviet head of state Mikhail Kalinin.

South Korean popular music genre. It emerged in the 1990s as a youth subculture influenced by Western dance music, [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]], R&B and rock. The "rap dance" of the group Seo Taiji and Boys helped modernize the music industry, and in the late 1990s Lee Soo-man of SM Entertainment developed the idol system. Today K-pop commonly refers to the output of teen idol acts, chiefly girl groups and boy bands, which emphasize visual appeal and performance. In the 2010s the Korean Wave and social media drove its international popularity; in 2019 South Korea ranked sixth among music markets, led by [[BTS]] and [[Blackpink]]. The genre has been criticized for its commercialism and its treatment of artists, and the industry is dominated by four companies: SM, YG, JYP and Hybe.

Widely used climate classification dividing Earth's climates into five main groups. The groups are A ([[Tropical climate|tropical]]), B (arid), C (temperate), D (continental) and E (polar), and subgroups are given by letters for seasonal [[Precipitation|precipitation]] and [[Temperature|temperature]]. For example, Af indicates a tropical rainforest climate and Cfb an oceanic climate with warm summers. Wladimir Köppen first published it in 1884 and designed it from his experience as a botanist, so its main groups reflect vegetation types. Rudolf Geiger revised it in 1954 and 1961, which is why it is sometimes called the Köppen–Geiger climate classification. The Trewartha system modified it in 1966 to create a more refined middle-latitude zone.

Conventional definition of the edge of space, 100 kilometers above [[Sea level|mean sea level]]. It is named after Theodore von Kármán, who calculated a theoretical limit of 83.8 km (52.1 mi) for [[Airplane|airplane]] flight. The line has no distinct physical significance, since the atmosphere changes gradually across it. The record-keeping body FAI uses it to separate aeronautics from astronautics. It is mainly used for legal purposes, distinguishing [[Spacecraft|spacecraft]] from aircraft, and international law does not define where airspace ends.

Ancient Indian natural scientist and philosopher who founded the Vaisheshika school of [[Indian philosophy]]. Little is known of his life, and the century in which he lived remains debated. The school explains the universe through an [[Atom|atomic]] theory, applying logic and realism, and it is among the earliest known systematic realist [[Ontology|ontologies]]. Its foundational text, the *Vaiśeṣika Sūtra*, argues that subdivision must end in eternal, indivisible smallest entities (*paramāṇu*) that combine to form complex substances. The school represents the earliest Indian [[Physics|physics]]. It describes six categories of reality, including substance, quality and action, and claims these are sufficient to describe everything in the universe.

Stone building at the center of the [[Masjid al-Haram]] in [[Mecca]], Saudi Arabia. Muslims regard it as the House of God, and it determines the qibla, the direction of prayer for Muslims worldwide. Circling it seven times counterclockwise, known as tawaf, is a required rite of the [[Hajj]] and umrah pilgrimages. According to Islamic tradition, it was rebuilt several times, most famously by Ibrahim and his son Ismail. The current structure was built after a fire during the Umayyad siege of Mecca in 683. The Black Stone, set into its eastern corner, is venerated; scientific examinations describe a composition resembling agate, basalt or impact glass, with a meteoritic origin unconfirmed.

Contact sport played by two teams of seven players each. A lone raider from one team enters the other half of the court and tries to tag defenders without being tackled. A single raid often lasts a maximum of 30 seconds. The raider scores for successful tags, while defenders score if the raider is tackled, goes out of bounds or is timed out. Tagged or tackled players are temporarily out until their team scores. The standard style, played on a rectangular court, is part of international competition such as the [[Asian Games]]; circle style, also called Punjabi kabaddi, is played on a circular field. The rules of modern kabaddi were formalized in India in the 1920s, and the sport is the national sport of Bangladesh.

Esoteric school of thought in Jewish mysticism. It interprets the [[Hebrew Bible]] and Rabbinic literature symbolically to reveal their hidden meaning. It emerged in 12th- to 13th-century Occitania and later spread to [[Spain]]. Its foundational text, the Zohar, was likely written by Rabbi Moses de León in the late 13th century. Isaac Luria, in the 16th century, is considered the father of contemporary Kabbalah, and his teachings were popularized through [[Hasidic Judaism]] from the 18th century onward.

Indian devotional mystic poet and saint. Born in [[Varanasi]] in what is now [[Uttar Pradesh]], he was a disciple of Ramananda, founder of the Ramanandi Sampradaya. His verses influenced [[Hinduism]]'s Bhakti movement and are included in the [[Guru Granth Sahib]], the scripture of [[Sikhism]]. Critical of organized religion, he questioned the practices of both [[Islam]] and Hinduism and was threatened by Hindus and Muslims during his lifetime. He taught that truth lies with those who see all things as divine and drop the ego. His poems, composed in a mix of dialects called Sadhukkadi, include couplets known as dohas. The Kabir panth, whose members are Kabir panthis, recognizes him as its founder.

Classical Japanese theatrical form mixing dramatic performance with traditional dance. It is known for stylized acting, elaborate costumes and kumadori makeup. Kabuki is thought to have originated in the early [[Edo period]], when [[Izumo no Okuni]] formed a female dance troupe that performed in [[Kyoto]]. Women were banned from performing in 1629, after which kabuki became an all-male form. It developed through the late 17th century and reached its zenith in the mid-18th century. Its [[Kanji|kanji]] can be read as 'sing', 'dance' and 'skill', but these ateji characters do not reflect its etymology, which probably derives from the verb kabuku, 'to lean' or 'to be out of the ordinary'. [[UNESCO]] proclaimed kabuki an intangible heritage in 2005 and inscribed it on its Representative List in 2008.

Capital and largest city of [[Afghanistan]]. It lies in a narrow valley of the [[Hindu Kush]] at 1,791 meters (5,876 ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capital cities in the world. Kabul is believed to be over 3,500 years old and was a key stop on the [[Silk Road]], at a crossroads between [[Central Asia]] and [[South Asia]]. Rulers of the [[Mughal Empire]] used it as a summer capital in the 16th century. It became the capital of Afghanistan under Timur Shah Durrani. In the 20th century it gained the nickname "Paris of Central Asia" as a stop on the hippie trail. The 1990s civil war destroyed much of the city, and the [[Taliban]] captured it in 1996 and again in 2021.

Capital of Kaduna State in north-western [[Nigeria]]. It was the political capital of Northern Nigeria, holding that status from 1917 until 1967, and it sits on the Kaduna River. British colonial authorities chose the site for its proximity to the [[Lagos]]–Kano Railway. The city's industries include textiles, which have declined, as well as machinery, steel, [[Petroleum|petroleum]] products and [[Bearing (mechanical)|bearings]]. Its refinery, one of Nigeria's four main oil refineries, is supplied by a pipeline from the Niger Delta. The Nigerian Defence Academy is also located in the city, and Kaduna International Airport has operated since 1982. The city also has an inland dry port.

Lebanese-American writer, poet and visual artist. Born in the village of Bsharri in the Ottoman-ruled Mount Lebanon region, he emigrated with his mother and siblings to the United States in 1895 and attended school in Boston. He studied art in [[Paris]] from 1908 to 1910 and settled in [[New York City]] in 1911. He is best known for *The Prophet* (1923), a series of sermonic essays on love, marriage and spirituality that has been translated into more than 100 languages. He wrote in both Arabic and English, and his paintings incorporated spiritual and mythological symbolism. He remains celebrated as a literary hero in Lebanon.

Japanese genre of giant monster films, usually depicting creatures attacking cities and battling the Japan Self-Defense Forces or other monsters. Its social and political commentary often reflected the times. The 1954 film *Godzilla* is credited with pioneering the subgenre, initially as a metaphor for [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]] after the [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]]. Other notable kaiju include Rodan, Mothra, King Ghidorah and Gamera.
